family_lesson.where_to_look_first: For the local mallow lesson, go to the flower center first: look for numerous stamens commonly fused into a staminal column around the style. Then confirm alternate/spiral usually stipulate leaves, often palmate venation, stellate hairs, a superior ovary and the fruit architecture.
family_lesson.strongest_local_pattern: Alternate stipulate leaves + stellate hairs + 5-part radial flower + many stamens fused into a tube/column + superior ovary + schizocarp/capsule or fleshy segmented fruit.
family_lesson.broad_family_correction: Broad Malvaceae includes lineages formerly treated as Tiliaceae, Sterculiaceae, Bombacaceae and others. Across the broad family, stamens may be free, fascicled or fused; petals may be reduced or absent; fruit may be a schizocarp, capsule, berry, drupe or samara. Therefore the classic Hibiscus/Callirhoe staminal-column look is a powerful local Malvoideae cue, not an absolute family definition.
authoritative_framework: Habit ranges from herbs and shrubs to trees and occasional lianas.
Leaves are commonly alternate or spiral and usually stipulate; venation is often palmate or 3-nerved from the base.
Stellate or lepidote hairs are frequent and are high-value supporting characters.
The ovary is superior in the common broad-family framework.
Within Malvoideae, epicalyx bracts may be present or absent and numerous stamens are commonly fused into a tube around the style.
Fruit architecture is diverse across broad Malvaceae.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not require an epicalyx; it can be present or absent.
Do not require a staminal column across every broad-Malvaceae lineage.
Do not require five showy spreading petals; Malvaviscus keeps its petals furled and sterculioid relatives can look very different.
Do not identify the family from stellate hairs alone.
Do not treat every mallow fruit as a dry schizocarp; Malvaviscus has a fleshy segmented fruit.

local_cards.role: canonical local family anchor and staminal-column lesson
key_points: Five red petals remain tightly furled rather than spreading flat.
The staminal column and style project conspicuously beyond the petals.
Leaves are cordate to shallowly lobed and commonly stellate-hairy.
Fruit becomes fleshy and segmented rather than a typical dry poppy-mallow schizocarp.
Shows the classic open radial mallow flower more clearly than Turk's cap.
Useful for epicalyx/calyx, staminal column and dry segmented-fruit sequence.
Preserve the project's no-epicalyx teaching cue.
Use it to prevent the learner from making an epicalyx mandatory for Malvaceae.

Cistaceae.tie_breaker: Both can present 5-petaled radial flowers with many stamens. In the common local Malvoideae pattern, look for stipules/stellate hairs plus stamens fused into a conspicuous tube or column and a segmented mallow fruit; Cistaceae commonly keeps the stamens free.

Geraniaceae.tie_breaker: Geraniaceae can be palmately veined and 5-parted, but lacks the classic mallow staminal tube and develops the distinctive beaked geranium-type fruit rather than the local mallow schizocarp/capsule pattern.

fast_key: Alternate/spiral stipulate leaf + stellate hairs -> consider Malvaceae.
5-part radial flower + many stamens fused into a column around the style -> strong local Malvoideae confirmation.
Open winecup flower + dry segmented mericarps -> Callirhoe-type anchor.
Furled red petals + long projecting staminal column + fleshy segmented fruit -> Turk's cap.
No epicalyx does not rule out Malvaceae.
A non-Hibiscus-looking broad-Malvaceae plant should be checked with leaf hairs, stipules, flower construction and ovary/fruit rather than rejected.
